title.en: Classify economic activities as business, profession and employment

say.en: A farmer sells rice, a teacher teaches, a doctor treats patients, and a mother cooks for her family. Only some of these are business. What makes the difference? In this lesson: Distinguish economic from non-economic activities.
Classify economic activities as business, profession and employment.
State the characteristics of business.

body.en: Human activities are *economic* when they are done to earn a living or to create wealth (a shopkeeper selling goods, an engineer designing a bridge for a fee) and non-economic when done for love, duty, religion or social service (a parent cooking for the family, volunteering at a temple). Economic activities are of three kinds: business (producing or exchanging goods and services for profit), profession (specialised services by trained people, under a code of conduct set by a professional body, for a fee) and employment (working for another under a contract for a wage or salary).

Economic: to earn a living.
Non-economic: love, duty, service.
Business, profession, employment.

title.en: On the board: characteristics of business

say.en: Business has these features.

text.en: characteristics of business
Economic activity, for profit
Production or purchase of goods and services for sale
Sale or exchange: not for one's own use
Dealings are regular, not one-off
Profit earning is the main purpose
Uncertainty of returns and an element of risk

say.en: So:

text.en: Selling your old bicycle once is not business
A shop selling bicycles every day is

explanation.en: Business trades or produces for profit; professions give expert services under a code of conduct; employment is working for an employer; love and service are non-economic.

say.en: Sort each activity.

body.en: They differ in how one enters them and what one earns. *Business* is started by an entrepreneur's decision and legal formalities, needs capital according to its size, earns profit and bears risk. A profession needs qualifications and membership of a professional body (the Bar Council, the Institute of Chartered Accountants), limited capital for an office, and earns a professional fee with moderate risk. Employment needs the qualifications the employer asks for, no capital, and earns a fixed salary or wage with little risk. Transfer of interest is possible in business but not in a profession or employment.

Employment: contract, salary, little risk.

problem.en: Is a person who sells his old car once a businessman? Justify.

steps.en: Business needs regular dealings in goods or services.
A single, isolated sale of a personal asset is not regular.
The car was bought for personal use, not for resale.
So it is not business; a used-car dealer who buys and sells cars regularly is.

answer.en: No: a one-off sale of a personal asset lacks regularity and the intention of trading for profit.
